questions.skill: Enforcing separation of duties in financial operations
questions.performanceIndicator: Design an approval workflow that prevents one person from completing a sensitive transaction alone
questions.scenarioContext: At a charitable foundation, one accounts-payable specialist can create a new vendor, change its banking details, and release payment without another person's review.
questions.prompt: Which change would BEST reduce the risk of fraud?

choices.A: Require independent approval for vendor changes and payment release
choices.B: Give the specialist a second account for high-value payments
choices.C: Increase the specialist's transaction limit to reduce processing delays
choices.D: Review only payments that recipients later dispute

questions.explanation: Independent approval separates incompatible duties so one individual cannot establish a payment destination and release funds without oversight. A second account does not create independence. A higher limit increases exposure, and reviewing only disputed transactions is reactive and may miss successful fraud.

questions.competency: VII.B — Foundational Operations Concepts, Resource Protection, and Incident Management
questions.skill: Using job rotation to expose concealed operational abuse
questions.performanceIndicator: Recognize how personnel rotation supports fraud detection and process resilience
questions.scenarioContext: A gaming company has allowed one operations employee to reconcile the same sensitive transaction queue for several years. Management is concerned that errors or manipulation could remain hidden because no one else performs the process.
questions.prompt: Which practice would MOST directly address this concern?

choices.A: Increase the employee's system privileges so reconciliation is faster
choices.B: Remove all logs after each reconciliation cycle
choices.C: Let the employee select a trusted substitute only when convenient
choices.D: Implement planned job rotation with independently assigned personnel

questions.explanation: Planned job rotation brings independent personnel into the function, increasing the chance that hidden errors or abuse will be identified while also reducing reliance on one employee. Additional privilege increases risk. Deleting logs removes evidence, and a substitute chosen only by the incumbent does not provide consistent independent scrutiny.

questions.competency: VII.B — Foundational Operations Concepts, Resource Protection, and Incident Management
questions.skill: Protecting removable backup media during off-site transport
questions.performanceIndicator: Select safeguards that preserve confidentiality and accountability while media is in transit
questions.scenarioContext: A medical research institute transports removable backup media to an off-site vault each week. The media contains sensitive study records and passes through a contracted courier before reaching controlled storage.
questions.prompt: Which THREE controls are MOST appropriate for this process? Select 3 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Write the media decryption key on the outside of the transport case
choices.B: Encrypt the media with keys managed separately from the shipment
choices.C: Use tamper-evident packaging and documented custody transfers
choices.D: Allow the courier to store delayed shipments at any convenient location
choices.E: Reconcile media identifiers and receipt records at the destination

questions.explanation: Encryption with separately controlled keys protects confidentiality, tamper-evident packaging and custody records support integrity and accountability, and destination reconciliation confirms that the correct media arrived. Placing a key on the case defeats encryption, while unapproved temporary storage breaks the controlled transport process.

questions.competency: VII.B — Foundational Operations Concepts, Resource Protection, and Incident Management
questions.skill: Containing compromised cloud access credentials
questions.performanceIndicator: Prioritize incident actions that stop active misuse while preserving investigation data
questions.scenarioContext: A travel services provider detects an access token being used from an unexpected location to download internal files. The legitimate user confirms that the activity is not theirs, and centralized audit records are available.
questions.prompt: What should the incident responder do FIRST?

choices.A: Wait for the token to expire naturally so the actor's behavior can be observed
choices.B: Revoke the token, contain related sessions, and preserve relevant audit evidence
choices.C: Delete the user's account and all files accessed with the token
choices.D: Restore the affected service from backup before limiting access

questions.explanation: Revoking the exposed credential and containing associated sessions stops active misuse, while preserving audit evidence supports scoping and investigation. Waiting prolongs exposure. Deleting the account and files can destroy evidence and disrupt legitimate work, and restoration does not address an attacker who still holds valid access.

questions.competency: VII.C — Detection, Prevention, Patch, and Change Management
questions.skill: Selecting detection controls for fragile operational technology
questions.performanceIndicator: Balance visibility with the availability constraints of a sensitive network
questions.scenarioContext: A water treatment facility needs better visibility into suspicious traffic on a legacy control network. Some controllers may fail if inline devices delay, block, or modify their communications.
questions.prompt: Which initial approach BEST addresses the requirement?

choices.A: Place an untested prevention device inline and enable automatic blocking
choices.B: Install host agents on every controller without compatibility testing
choices.C: Use passive network intrusion detection from monitored traffic copies
choices.D: Disable network monitoring to preserve controller availability

questions.explanation: Passive network intrusion detection can improve visibility without sitting inline or altering traffic, making it a prudent initial choice for availability-sensitive legacy systems. Untested inline prevention and host agents may disrupt operations. Disabling monitoring preserves neither visibility nor the ability to detect attacks.

questions.competency: VII.C — Detection, Prevention, Patch, and Change Management
questions.skill: Applying application allowlisting to fixed-function endpoints
questions.performanceIndicator: Choose a preventive control suited to a stable and narrowly defined workload
questions.scenarioContext: A museum operates public information kiosks that run a small, stable set of approved applications. Attackers have repeatedly tried to execute downloaded tools after escaping the kiosk interface.
questions.prompt: Which preventive measure would be MOST effective?

choices.A: Allow execution only for explicitly approved applications and supporting components
choices.B: Maintain a list containing only the malicious files already observed
choices.C: Permit all signed applications regardless of business need
choices.D: Rely solely on weekly review of kiosk event logs

questions.explanation: Application allowlisting is well suited to fixed-function kiosks because the legitimate software set is small and stable; unapproved downloaded tools are denied by default. A blocklist addresses only known files. Trusting every signed application exceeds need, and weekly log review is detective rather than preventive.

questions.competency: VII.C — Detection, Prevention, Patch, and Change Management
questions.skill: Prioritizing vulnerability remediation using environmental risk
questions.performanceIndicator: Rank remediation based on exposure, exploitability, asset value, and compensating controls
questions.scenarioContext: A retailer finds the same high-severity software flaw on an isolated training server and on an internet-facing order system that processes sensitive customer data. The order system has no effective compensating control, while the training server is scheduled for retirement.
questions.prompt: How should the vulnerability manager prioritize remediation?

choices.A: Patch the training server first because it is easier to schedule
choices.B: Assign identical deadlines because the technical severity is the same
choices.C: Defer both systems until the next annual maintenance cycle
choices.D: Prioritize the order system based on exposure, business impact, and lack of mitigation

questions.explanation: Technical severity is only one input to remediation priority. The internet-facing order system combines exposure, valuable data, business criticality, and no effective mitigation, so it represents the greater environmental risk. Convenience, identical deadlines, and annual deferral fail to account for those material differences.

questions.competency: VII.C — Detection, Prevention, Patch, and Change Management
questions.skill: Responding to an unauthorized production configuration change
questions.performanceIndicator: Restore control while preserving evidence and service stability
questions.scenarioContext: Continuous monitoring detects a new firewall rule that permits broad inbound access to a production database segment. No approved change record exists, but immediately deleting the rule could interrupt a business process whose owner has not yet been identified.
questions.prompt: What is the BEST next action?

choices.A: Leave the rule indefinitely because removing it might affect operations
choices.B: Invoke the unauthorized-change procedure, assess exposure and dependency, then contain or roll back safely
choices.C: Create a retroactive approval record without investigating who added the rule
choices.D: Disable firewall logging so additional unrecorded changes do not generate alerts

questions.explanation: The unauthorized-change process should preserve evidence, determine risk and operational dependency, and support timely containment or safe rollback. Leaving broad access in place prolongs exposure. Retroactive approval conceals a control failure, while disabling logging destroys visibility and accountability.

questions.competency: VII.D — Recovery Strategies and Disaster Recovery Processes
questions.skill: Designing backup frequency to meet a recovery point objective
questions.performanceIndicator: Translate acceptable data loss into a suitable protection interval
questions.scenarioContext: A reservation system has a recovery point objective of 15 minutes. Its current nightly backup process could require the business to recreate nearly a full day of transactions after a failure.
questions.prompt: Which improvement MOST directly supports the stated objective?

choices.A: Increase the recovery time objective to twenty-four hours
choices.B: Move the nightly copy to a storage device with greater capacity
choices.C: Capture transaction changes at intervals that limit data loss to 15 minutes or less
choices.D: Perform an annual walkthrough of the recovery contact list

questions.explanation: The recovery point objective defines the maximum tolerable amount of recent data loss, so the protection method must capture changes frequently enough to keep that loss within 15 minutes. Storage capacity does not determine data currency. Changing the recovery time objective addresses downtime rather than data loss, and a contact-list walkthrough does not improve the restore point.

questions.competency: VII.D — Recovery Strategies and Disaster Recovery Processes
questions.skill: Implementing fault tolerance for a critical network service
questions.performanceIndicator: Select a design that continues service after a component failure
questions.scenarioContext: An emergency communications center relies on one network gateway. A gateway hardware failure currently disconnects dispatch workstations until technicians install a replacement.
questions.prompt: Which solution would BEST improve fault tolerance?

choices.A: Deploy redundant gateways with automatic state-aware failover and test the failover process
choices.B: Keep a configuration manual in a locked cabinet near the gateway
choices.C: Purchase a replacement gateway that remains unopened at another facility
choices.D: Extend the retention period for gateway traffic logs

questions.explanation: Redundant gateways with automatic, tested failover allow service to continue when one component fails. Documentation and an unopened spare may speed manual recovery but still permit an outage. Longer log retention supports investigation, not continuity of the gateway service.

questions.competency: VII.D — Recovery Strategies and Disaster Recovery Processes
questions.skill: Reducing correlated risk across multiple processing sites
questions.performanceIndicator: Evaluate geographic and utility dependencies in a multisite recovery design
questions.scenarioContext: A securities clearing organization operates two active processing sites in the same metropolitan area. Both use different buildings but depend on the same electrical substation and telecommunications exchange.
questions.prompt: Which change would provide the GREATEST resilience against a regional disruption?

choices.A: Add more servers to each existing site without changing external dependencies
choices.B: Assign separate facility names to distinguish the two locations in documentation
choices.C: Move both sites onto different floors of the newer building
choices.D: Establish processing capacity in a geographically separated area with independent utility paths

questions.explanation: Geographic separation and independent utility paths reduce the correlated risks that could disable both current sites at once. More servers do not help if shared external services fail. Naming changes have no operational effect, and colocating the sites in one building increases common-mode exposure.

questions.competency: VII.D — Recovery Strategies and Disaster Recovery Processes
questions.skill: Planning a simulation-based disaster recovery exercise
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify the features and outcomes of a scenario-driven recovery simulation
questions.scenarioContext: An insurance company wants cross-functional teams to respond to a realistic data-center outage scenario, make recovery decisions as conditions evolve, and identify coordination gaps without switching production services.
questions.prompt: Which THREE elements belong in the proposed exercise? Select 3 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: A complete unannounced shutdown of the production data center
choices.B: A defined scenario with timed operational developments
choices.C: Participation by business, technology, facilities, and communications roles
choices.D: A requirement to make recovered systems serve live customer traffic
choices.E: Documented observations, decisions, gaps, and assigned corrective actions

questions.explanation: A simulation uses a realistic scenario and evolving inputs to exercise cross-functional decision-making without disrupting production. Capturing gaps and assigning corrective actions turns observations into improvement. Shutting down production or serving live traffic would introduce the operational risk of more disruptive test types and is not required for this objective.

questions.competency: VII.E — Business Continuity Planning, Physical Security, and Personnel Safety
questions.skill: Accounting for personnel during an emergency evacuation
questions.performanceIndicator: Prioritize life safety and reliable accountability procedures
questions.scenarioContext: During a warehouse evacuation drill, supervisors cannot determine whether contractors working in remote loading areas reached the assembly point. Badge records show entry but do not reliably reflect current location or exit.
questions.prompt: Which improvement should receive the HIGHEST priority?

choices.A: Require contractors to recover company equipment before leaving the building
choices.B: Implement inclusive muster, accountability, and escalation procedures for employees and contractors
choices.C: Delay evacuation until supervisors reconcile all badge records indoors
choices.D: Limit future drills to office employees so results are easier to measure

questions.explanation: Emergency procedures must account for everyone on site through defined assembly, reporting, and escalation methods that work for employees and contractors. Equipment recovery and indoor reconciliation can delay evacuation and endanger personnel. Excluding contractors from drills leaves the identified life-safety gap unresolved.

questions.competency: VII.E — Business Continuity Planning, Physical Security, and Personnel Safety
questions.skill: Controlling escorted visitor access to a data center
questions.performanceIndicator: Apply physical access controls that authenticate, constrain, and record visitor activity
questions.scenarioContext: A data center permits maintenance vendors to enter equipment rooms after signing a paper log. A recent review found that visitors sometimes separate from their escorts and remain in restricted areas after their scheduled work ends.
questions.prompt: What is the BEST corrective measure?

choices.A: Allow vendors to borrow employee badges so doors do not delay maintenance
choices.B: Replace the paper log with a camera but permit unescorted movement
choices.C: Issue time-limited visitor credentials, enforce escort rules, and reconcile exit
choices.D: Give recurring vendors permanent access to all equipment rooms

questions.explanation: Time-limited visitor credentials, enforced escorts, and exit reconciliation constrain access to the authorized period and preserve accountability. Borrowed employee badges undermine attribution. Cameras are detective and do not replace access restrictions, while permanent broad access exceeds the vendors' temporary need.

questions.competency: VII.E — Business Continuity Planning, Physical Security, and Personnel Safety
questions.skill: Preparing personnel for higher-risk business travel
questions.performanceIndicator: Select proportionate travel security measures that protect people and information
questions.scenarioContext: Executives from a renewable energy company will visit a region where device searches, theft, and targeted social engineering are credible concerns. They need limited access to current business documents during the trip.
questions.prompt: Which preparation is MOST appropriate?

choices.A: Provide a travel briefing, minimally provisioned devices, limited data access, and a check-in and incident process
choices.B: Let travelers use their normal devices with complete archives for convenience
choices.C: Require travelers to conceal incidents until they return to avoid disrupting the trip
choices.D: Publish the itinerary and contact details broadly so colleagues can monitor progress

questions.explanation: A tailored briefing, minimally provisioned devices, restricted data access, and clear communications and incident procedures reduce both personnel and information risk while supporting the business need. Full archives increase exposure, delayed reporting impedes response, and broad itinerary publication can create additional targeting risk.

questions.competency: VIII.A — Security in the Software Development Life Cycle
questions.skill: Defining testable security requirements in a Waterfall project
questions.performanceIndicator: Translate policy objectives into traceable requirements and acceptance criteria before design approval
questions.scenarioContext: A public benefits agency is beginning a Waterfall development project. Its requirements document says only that the application must protect confidential information, and the design phase is scheduled to begin next week.
questions.prompt: What should the security architect do FIRST?

choices.A: Schedule a penetration test after implementation and use its findings to define the missing requirements.
choices.B: Let each developer interpret the policy statement and document the selected controls in source-code comments.
choices.C: Convert applicable risks and policies into measurable security requirements, acceptance criteria, and requirements traceability before design approval.
choices.D: Defer security requirements until user acceptance testing reveals which functions handle confidential information.

questions.explanation: In a sequential lifecycle, measurable security requirements and acceptance criteria should be established before design so they can guide architecture, implementation, and testing. A late penetration test can validate controls but is not a substitute for requirements. Individual interpretations create inconsistency, and waiting for acceptance testing makes fundamental security defects costly to correct.

questions.competency: VIII.A — Security in the Software Development Life Cycle
questions.skill: Establishing a baseline for software process maturity improvement
questions.performanceIndicator: Use current-state assessment to prioritize sustainable process improvements
questions.scenarioContext: A logistics company wants to improve software security maturity. Different teams use unrelated checklists, metrics are unavailable, and leaders disagree about which process weaknesses create the greatest business risk.
questions.prompt: Which action is the BEST starting point for a sustainable improvement program?

choices.A: Assess current capabilities against a selected maturity model, define the desired state, and prioritize gaps according to business risk.
choices.B: Mandate the highest maturity level for every team before documenting existing development processes.
choices.C: Purchase additional testing tools and use the number of generated findings as the maturity score.
choices.D: Standardize the easiest existing checklist without determining whether it addresses the organization's principal risks.

questions.explanation: A maturity initiative needs an evidence-based current-state baseline, a business-aligned target, and prioritized gaps. Declaring the highest level without understanding existing processes is unrealistic. Tool output alone does not measure institutionalized capability, and adopting the easiest checklist may standardize practices that do not address material risk.

questions.competency: VIII.A — Security in the Software Development Life Cycle
questions.skill: Performing security impact analysis for a significant application change
questions.performanceIndicator: Determine when system changes require updated risk assessment and control validation
questions.scenarioContext: An insurer plans to add a partner-facing interface to an internally used claims application. The change introduces external data flows and a new category of personal information, but the project manager considers it a routine feature release.
questions.prompt: What is the security manager's MOST appropriate response?

choices.A: Approve the release because the underlying application previously passed its security evaluation.
choices.B: Require the partner to accept all application risk because the new interface will be used externally.
choices.C: Repeat every historical test regardless of whether the affected controls or data flows changed.
choices.D: Conduct a security impact analysis and update the risk assessment, control validation, and authorization evidence as the change requires.

questions.explanation: New exposure and data use can alter the system's risk profile, so the organization should analyze the change and reassess affected controls before release. Prior evaluation does not automatically cover materially different data flows. Risk accountability cannot simply be transferred to the partner, while repeating every test without scoping wastes effort and may still miss change-specific risk.

questions.competency: VIII.A — Security in the Software Development Life Cycle
questions.skill: Applying proportional security controls to rapid prototypes
questions.performanceIndicator: Preserve experimentation while preventing prototype shortcuts from becoming production risk
questions.scenarioContext: A research team wants to demonstrate a new customer analytics concept in three weeks. To save time, it proposes using a copy of production data and connecting the prototype directly to an internal production service. Executives say the demonstration may later become a supported application.
questions.prompt: Which approach BEST balances rapid learning with secure development?

choices.A: Permit unrestricted production access because the prototype will initially have few users.
choices.B: Use minimized or synthetic data in an isolated environment, define prototype security constraints, and require full lifecycle review before any production transition.
choices.C: Treat the prototype as production-ready if its functional demonstration succeeds within the deadline.
choices.D: Prohibit prototyping and require the team to complete the entire production release process before testing the concept.

questions.explanation: Isolation, safe data, and explicit constraints reduce experimentation risk, while a defined transition gate prevents temporary shortcuts from entering production unnoticed. Few users do not eliminate data or service risk. Functional success is not security assurance, and banning prototypes sacrifices legitimate learning when proportionate controls can contain exposure.

questions.competency: VIII.A — Security in the Software Development Life Cycle
questions.skill: Evaluating evidence for a controlled application release
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify the evidence needed to make an informed change approval decision
questions.scenarioContext: A regional utility is preparing a normal release that changes authorization logic in a customer portal. The change advisory group must decide whether the release is ready for production.
questions.prompt: Which TWO items provide the MOST relevant security evidence for the approval decision? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: The number of lines of code written by each developer during the release.
choices.B: A documented security impact analysis identifying affected assets, threats, and controls.
choices.C: A statement that the release compiled successfully on the lead developer's workstation.
choices.D: A list of unrelated defects deferred from older versions of the application.
choices.E: Results of risk-appropriate testing plus an approved deployment and rollback plan.

questions.explanation: The impact analysis explains how the authorization change affects risk, while relevant test results and controlled deployment and rollback plans show whether the change can be introduced safely. Code volume is not evidence of security. A local compilation demonstrates little about control effectiveness, and unrelated historical defects do not establish this release's readiness.

questions.competency: VIII.B — Security Controls in Development Ecosystems and Secure Coding
questions.skill: Controlling integrated development environment extensions
questions.performanceIndicator: Reduce development endpoint and source-code exposure through governed tooling
questions.scenarioContext: A game studio discovers that an unapproved integrated development environment extension copied portions of proprietary source code to an external service. Developers currently install extensions without review because they improve productivity.
questions.prompt: Which control would BEST reduce recurrence while supporting legitimate development needs?

choices.A: Maintain an approved extension catalog, validate source and permissions, centrally enforce installation policy, and monitor exceptions.
choices.B: Permit any digitally signed marketplace extension because the signature establishes that its behavior is safe.
choices.C: Rely on endpoint data loss prevention rules while allowing developers to install extensions from any source.
choices.D: Review an extension's source and permissions only after monitoring identifies suspicious outbound activity.

questions.explanation: A governed catalog with provenance, permission review, technical enforcement, and exception monitoring addresses extension supply-chain risk without eliminating useful tools. A signature establishes origin and integrity, not safe behavior. Data loss prevention is only a partial safeguard, and reviewing an extension after suspicious activity is reactive rather than preventive.

questions.competency: VIII.B — Security Controls in Development Ecosystems and Secure Coding
questions.skill: Preventing stored cross-site scripting through contextual output handling
questions.performanceIndicator: Select source-level controls that prevent stored data from becoming executable browser content
questions.scenarioContext: A community platform stores user profile text in a database. When another user views a profile, the application inserts that text directly into an HTML page, allowing stored script content to execute in the viewer's browser.
questions.prompt: What is the BEST primary remediation?

choices.A: Encrypt the profile table so scripts cannot be read directly from database storage.
choices.B: Require longer passwords for users who are permitted to edit profile text.
choices.C: Apply context-appropriate output encoding and safe templating, supplemented by server-side input validation where suitable.
choices.D: Hide the profile editing link from users whose browsers do not support client-side scripting.

questions.explanation: Context-aware output encoding prevents stored untrusted text from being interpreted as executable markup or script, and safe templating helps apply that control consistently. Input validation can provide defense in depth but should not replace encoding at the output context. Database encryption, password length, and hidden interface links do not neutralize malicious content rendered to an authorized viewer.

questions.competency: VIII.B — Security Controls in Development Ecosystems and Secure Coding
questions.skill: Implementing secure application error handling
questions.performanceIndicator: Preserve diagnostic value without exposing internal details to users
questions.scenarioContext: A laboratory scheduling application returns database statements, internal file paths, and stack traces to users when requests fail. Developers rely on these messages to troubleshoot production incidents.
questions.prompt: How should the development team correct this weakness?

choices.A: Continue displaying the details but add a notice telling users not to share error messages.
choices.B: Suppress all error records so internal implementation details are not retained anywhere.
choices.C: Send stack traces only to users who confirm that they work for the organization.
choices.D: Return generic client messages with correlation identifiers and record detailed diagnostics in protected, access-controlled logs.

questions.explanation: Generic responses prevent disclosure of internal structure, while correlation identifiers connect user reports to detailed server-side logs available to authorized support staff. A warning does not protect exposed data. Eliminating logs impairs investigation, and employment status alone does not establish a user's operational need for sensitive diagnostic details.

questions.competency: VIII.B — Security Controls in Development Ecosystems and Secure Coding
questions.skill: Mitigating server-side request forgery in an application feature
questions.performanceIndicator: Constrain server-initiated requests to approved destinations and schemes
questions.scenarioContext: A document service accepts a user-supplied URL and instructs its server to retrieve the referenced file. Testing shows that crafted URLs can cause requests to internal administration endpoints and cloud instance metadata addresses.
questions.prompt: Which design change would MOST effectively reduce this risk?

choices.A: Reject hostnames on a block list of currently known internal services while allowing all other destinations.
choices.B: Restrict destinations and protocols with server-side allow lists, safely resolve and validate addresses, and block access to internal and metadata ranges.
choices.C: Route requests through an outbound proxy that records destinations but does not enforce a destination policy.
choices.D: Validate the initially resolved address but permit redirects without applying the validation again.

questions.explanation: Server-side destination controls, robust parsing and resolution, and explicit blocks for internal and metadata addresses constrain where the trusted server can connect. A block list can miss aliases and newly exposed destinations. Logging without enforcement detects but does not prevent access, and redirects must be revalidated because they can resolve to a forbidden target after the initial check.

questions.competency: VIII.B — Security Controls in Development Ecosystems and Secure Coding
questions.skill: Isolating continuous integration jobs that process untrusted contributions
questions.performanceIndicator: Apply least privilege and workload isolation to build automation
questions.scenarioContext: An open collaboration project runs proposed code changes from external contributors on a persistent continuous integration worker. The worker has network access to internal services and holds credentials used for production releases.
questions.prompt: What is the BEST way to reduce the resulting development ecosystem risk?

choices.A: Run untrusted jobs in ephemeral isolated workers without production secrets or unnecessary internal access, and use a separate trusted release stage.
choices.B: Keep the persistent worker and limit the production credential to the permissions normally required for a release.
choices.C: Scan proposed code before execution while retaining the worker's internal connectivity and production secrets.
choices.D: Run external contributions under a separate operating system account on the same persistent worker with access to the same network and secrets.

questions.explanation: Ephemeral isolation limits persistence and lateral movement, removal of production secrets enforces least privilege, and a separate trusted release stage prevents unreviewed code from inheriting deployment authority. Narrowing a release credential does not justify exposing it to untrusted jobs. Scanning is valuable but cannot replace containment, and a separate account on the same privileged worker may still reach shared secrets and internal services.

questions.competency: VIII.C — Assessing Software Security and Acquired Software Risk
questions.skill: Selecting interactive application security testing for runtime code analysis
questions.performanceIndicator: Match IAST capabilities to an instrumented test environment and existing functional tests
questions.scenarioContext: A pharmacy software team has extensive automated functional tests. It wants security findings that combine knowledge of executing code paths, data flow, and runtime behavior without waiting for a separate end-of-cycle scan.
questions.prompt: Which testing technique BEST fits this requirement?

choices.A: Static application security testing performed after each build without executing the application.
choices.B: Dynamic application security testing that probes exposed interfaces without internal runtime instrumentation.
choices.C: Interactive application security testing through instrumentation while the functional tests exercise the application.
choices.D: A manual penetration test conducted against the completed application at the end of the release cycle.

questions.explanation: IAST instruments the application during execution and can correlate runtime behavior with code and data flow while existing functional tests exercise relevant paths. SAST provides code insight without runtime observation, while DAST observes exposed behavior without the requested internal instrumentation. An end-of-cycle penetration test provides useful assurance but not continuous feedback during the automated functional tests.

questions.competency: VIII.C — Assessing Software Security and Acquired Software Risk
questions.skill: Evaluating lifecycle risk before acquiring commercial software
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify supplier commitments and lifecycle evidence that support ongoing risk management
questions.scenarioContext: A transit authority is evaluating commercial software for a system expected to remain in service for eight years. The application will support a critical business process and cannot be replaced quickly if the supplier ends support.
questions.prompt: Which TWO factors are MOST important to evaluate before acquisition? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Documented support and end-of-life plans, including expected maintenance for the required service period.
choices.B: A point-in-time penetration test summary for a demonstration version with no commitment to address future findings.
choices.C: A current security certification that does not define product support, update, or vulnerability handling obligations.
choices.D: Contractual vulnerability notification, remediation, update, and security incident obligations.
choices.E: A one-time source-code review performed before deployment with no provision for later versions or maintenance releases.

questions.explanation: Support and end-of-life plans reveal whether the product can remain maintainable across the intended service period, while contractual security obligations establish how vulnerabilities, updates, and incidents will be handled. Point-in-time tests, certifications, and code reviews may provide useful evidence about one version, but without ongoing commitments they do not manage security across the required eight-year lifecycle.

questions.competency: VIII.C — Assessing Software Security and Acquired Software Risk
questions.skill: Using a software bill of materials for vulnerability exposure analysis
questions.performanceIndicator: Trace a disclosed component vulnerability across deployed products and transitive dependencies
questions.scenarioContext: A vulnerability is disclosed in a common compression component. An industrial company uses dozens of internally developed and acquired applications, and the component may be included indirectly within other packages.
questions.prompt: Which capability would MOST improve the company's ability to determine its exposure quickly?

choices.A: A list of application owners that omits component and version information.
choices.B: A maintained software bill of materials linked to deployed versions and including direct and transitive dependencies.
choices.C: An external vulnerability scan of application endpoints that cannot identify components embedded inside packages.
choices.D: Supplier statements that deployed products are current without an inventory of included component versions.

questions.explanation: A current SBOM tied to deployed versions provides the component and dependency relationships needed to identify affected software, including indirect inclusion. Owner lists help coordination but cannot establish technical exposure without component data. External scans may not reveal packaged dependencies, and general supplier statements do not provide the component-version detail needed for rapid correlation.

questions.competency: VIII.C — Assessing Software Security and Acquired Software Risk
questions.skill: Preventing API mass assignment vulnerabilities
questions.performanceIndicator: Restrict client-modifiable object properties and enforce authorization on sensitive state changes
questions.scenarioContext: An API automatically maps every property in a client request to an internal account object. A tester adds an undocumented privilege property to an otherwise valid profile update and changes the account's role.
questions.prompt: Which remediation MOST directly addresses the coding weakness?

choices.A: Document the privilege property so clients know that it should not be changed.
choices.B: Require the tester to use a longer access token when sending profile updates.
choices.C: Rename sensitive internal properties so ordinary clients are less likely to guess them.
choices.D: Bind only explicitly permitted request fields and enforce server-side authorization for every sensitive property change.

questions.explanation: Explicit field allow-listing prevents arbitrary client properties from being bound to trusted objects, and authorization checks protect legitimate sensitive update paths. Documentation and obscure names do not enforce security. Token length relates to credential strength, not whether an authenticated client may modify a privileged field.

questions.competency: VIII.C — Assessing Software Security and Acquired Software Risk
questions.skill: Applying fuzz testing to a complex file parser
questions.performanceIndicator: Select a testing method suited to unexpected and malformed input combinations
questions.scenarioContext: A records-management product accepts complex files from untrusted external parties. Reviewers are concerned that unusual combinations of lengths, headers, and nested structures could trigger crashes or unsafe parser behavior that ordinary test cases do not cover.
questions.prompt: Which assessment method would BEST target this concern?

choices.A: Perform a manual source review focused on documented parsing paths and expected file structures.
choices.B: Run load tests using a large collection of well-formed files that follow the published specification.
choices.C: Use coverage-guided fuzz testing with malformed and mutated inputs while monitoring for crashes and anomalous behavior.
choices.D: Repeat functional acceptance tests with representative valid files and compare the resulting records.

questions.explanation: Fuzz testing systematically exercises unexpected input combinations and is well suited to finding parser crashes, boundary errors, and unsafe behavior outside ordinary functional cases. Manual review can help but may miss complex input interactions. Load and functional tests using valid files assess performance and expected behavior rather than resilience to malformed structures.
